items.title: October 2026 CPI: Inflation Firms, December Fed Hike Looms
items.description: October 2026 CPI: Inflation Firms, December Fed Hike Looms By Jake Krimmel Nov 10, 2026 October's consumer price index came in a touch hotter than forecasters expected, with headline inflation up 0.4% on the month and core up 0.3%. Because of last year's government shutdown, BLS did not publish annual rates, but the details show inflation remains broad-based. December Fed hike odds jumped to 99% and the 10-year Treasury yield moved higher, putting new upward pressure on mortgage rates after three straight weekly declines. Here's what today's report means for the Fed, consumers, and the housing market. October 2026 CPI at a Glance Headline CPI: +0.4% MoM Seasonally Adjusted (SA), following September's +0.6% rise, versus forecasts of +0.2% to +0.3%; BLS did not publish an annual rate because October 2025 data were not collected during the government shutdown Core CPI (less food & energy): +0.3% MoM (SA), matching September and August, versus a forecast of +0.2% Energy: +0.7% MoM (SA) after +5.2% in September; gasoline +1.0% MoM (SA) and +37.4% YoY Food: +0.5% MoM (SA), with food at home up 0.4% and food away from home up 0.5% Shelter: +0.3% MoM (SA) after +0.4% in September, with rent up 0.2% and owners' equivalent rent up 0.3% Real earnings: real average hourly earnings were unchanged, as 0.4% wage growth matched 0.4% inflation Fed outlook: odds of a December hike jumped to 99%, with Governor Waller's comments putting a 50 basis point move on the table Market reaction: the 10-year Treasury yield was up 9 basis points 25 minutes after the release Mortgage rates: Freddie Mac's 30-year rate fell to 7.18% in the week of November 5, the third straight weekly decline, after peaking at 7.4% in October October CPI: a touch hotter than expected, and inflation remains broad-based October’s CPI came in a touch hotter than consensus, with headline up 0.4% month over month (versus a forecasted 0.2 to 0.3%) and core inflation rising 0.3% month over month compared to an expected 0.2%. These figures hardly qualify as a shock to markets or the outlook, but the details of the report show inflation remains broad-based, with food, energy, shelter, and vehicles all up, to name a few. The BLS did not publish annual rates because of last year’s government shutdown, but headline inflation likely remains in the high 3s. These are the costs most salient to consumers and voters, as we saw, yet the Fed has less direct control over them. What it means for the Fed: a December hike looks almost certain The same supply-side and geopolitical pressures are still at work, with energy playing an important role and tariff-driven goods inflation not going away. These are the costs most salient to consumers and voters, as we saw, yet the Fed has less direct control over them. On the Fed outlook, a December hike now looks almost certain, with odds jumping to 99% this morning . That market reaction is both due to the warmer than anticipated CPI print and Governor Waller’s comments (which occurred prior to the CPI report) putting a 50 basis point move on the table for December. Additional hikes in early 2027 look more in play as well, with the 10-year Treasury up 9 basis points just 25 minutes after the CPI report release. What it means for housing: mortgage rates could turn higher again For housing in the near term, we could see upward pressure on mortgage rates again. After three straight weekly declines to 7.18% , rising Treasury yields and growing speculation about hikes in early 2027 could reverse that trend. October’s spike to 7.4% showed how quickly higher rates hurt demand, with contract signings and new listings each falling about 10% from September as buyers and sellers pulled back . Rate swings grab the headlines and matter for the marginal buyer, but the real wage squeeze is a longer-run, underexplored headwind for demand. Real average hourly earnings were flat in October as 0.4% wage growth matched 0.4% inflation, leaving annual real wage growth negative for buyers already facing mortgage rates above 7% .

items.title: VA Loans in a High-Rate Market: Lower Down Payments, Lower Costs
items.description: VA Loans in a High-Rate Market: Lower Down Payments, Lower Costs By Jiayi Xu Nov 10, 2026 Highlights: VA home loans –a benefit created by the Servicemen’s Readjustment Act of 1944–enable qualified borrowers with smaller down payments, more flexible credit terms, and lower interest rates, making it easier to access homeownership. The zero down payment option and lower down payments in general are a key advantage that VA loans offer. Over the past 12 months, more than 3 in 4 (75.7%) home sales with VA loans had a 0% down payment and nearly 9 in 10 (86.1%) VA loan home sales had a down payment below 10%. In contrast, the share of lower down payment conforming loan home sales was less than half as large. Just 2 in 5 (41.1%) home sales backed by conforming loans featured down payment rates below 10%. VA loans exhibit flexibility in their credit criteria. Nearly 1 in 4 (24.3% of) recent VA loan borrowers had Fair credit scores (vs. roughly 1 in 30 or 4.8% for conforming loan borrowers). For every credit score grouping, recent VA borrowers had lower down payments as a percent of purchase price than conforming loan borrowers. VA loans reduce payments through lower mortage rates, which is especially notable in a high-rate market Thanks to the lower interest rate, a 0% down VA loan not only shortens the time to homeownership by about four years, but its monthly payment is nearly the same as a conforming loan with 10% down. Scenarios where VA and conforming loans with the same down payment shares are considered (under 20%), result in even greater payment savings. In recognition of Veterans Day, Realtor.com® has undertaken a research initiative to highlight the benefits of VA mortgage loans for military households and the industry professionals who support them. Our analysis features a comprehensive comparison of key factors such as down payment requirements, credit score considerations, and mortgage rates, contrasting them with conforming loans originated in the past 12 months. In addition, we calculate the potential monthly savings that veteran households can gain from utilizing VA loans. With this research, we hope to empower veteran households with the knowledge and tools they need to make informed decisions about their homeownership goals and financial well-being. More information can be found at realtor.com/veterans as well as in the Veterans & Military Benefit section of for-sale home listings on Realtor.com . No downpayment VA loans help homebuyers clear the biggest hurdle Homeownership is harder to reach for first-time buyers than it has been in years. The median age of first-time buyers rose to 40, and their share of home purchases fell to a historic low of 21%. Saving for a down payment is a central obstacle. According to the Realtor.com site visitor survey, about one-third of first-time buyers say not having enough money for a down payment makes buying a home challenging. The standout benefit of VA loans is the ability to buy a home without the burden of a down payment, a game changer in today’s real estate market where home prices remain elevated . According to Realtor.com Economics analysis of newly released data from the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances , about 11% of renter households under 40 have qualified income to afford a median-priced home but lack the liquid savings for a 10% down payment. 1 For this group, a zero-down option such as a VA loan (for eligible borrowers) would address the upfront barrier directly. Another 83% of renter households under 40 are constrained by both savings and income. For them, a zero-down VA loan could also help eligible households reach homeownership sooner, but they would also need income growth or other assistance before they can buy. Over the past year, the average down payment percentage for VA loans stood at 4.3%, whereas the average down payment percentage for conforming loans was 19.1%. 2 Notably, nearly 9 in 10 (86.1%) VA loan recipients were able to secure homes with a down payment lower than 10%, while only 41.1% of homebuyers with conforming loans fell into this category. In fact, nearly 3 in 4 (75.7%) VA loans had a down payment of 0%—a feature not available with conforming loans. This highlights the significant benefit VA loans provide to those looking to achieve homeownership: no upfront funds needed. This is especially important for first-time homebuyers who lack historically high home equity to tap . However, according to a recent survey conducted by Veterans United, only 3 in 10 veterans were aware of the zero down payment benefits of VA loans . According to the Realtor.com site visitor survey, about 20% of first time homebuyers say that a low credit score makes buying a home difficult. Over the past year, nearly one in four (24.3%) homebuyers with VA loans fell into the Fair credit score category (580–669) compared with just 4.8% (roughly one in twenty) among conforming loan borrowers in the past year. 3 Figure 2: VA Borrowers Are More Likely To Have a Lower Credit Score Additionally, it’s important to highlight that the average down payment percentage for VA loans consistently remains lower than that for conforming loans, as seen in Figure 3. This trend is particularly evident among the roughly 1 in 4 VA borrowers with lower credit scores, those falling below the Good level (below 670). This advantage is especially beneficial for younger homebuyers who may face challenges, lacking both strong credit scores and the substantial down payment funds typically needed for their first home purchase. items.title: October Jobs Report: Surging Payrolls and Hiring Uptick Means Fed Hawks Can Exhale
items.description: October Jobs Report: Surging Payrolls and Hiring Uptick Means Fed Hawks Can Exhale By Jake Krimmel Nov 06, 2026 October Payrolls Jump 165,000, More Than Double Expectations, With 84,000 Jobs Revised Up Today’s October jobs report was impressive. Coming in, we would have been happy with the forecasted 65,000, more than double last month’s. Instead we got more than double those expectations, with payrolls up 165,000. Revisions added another 84,000 jobs to August and September, lifting the three-month average to 137,000 from about 51,000 a month ago. The unemployment rate slipped to 4.1%, just as the Chicago Fed predicted , while labor force participation rose to 61.9%, above the 61.8% expected. Both moved just a smidge, but together they are notable. Wages firmed too, up 0.4% in the month and 3.1% from a year ago, versus 3.0% in September. This is still a low hire, low fire market overall, but we could be seeing some green shoots on the hiring side. The numbers could still be revised, of course, and the trend matters more than any one point; but you don’t get a good trend without a good month. A Strong Report Clears the Way for the Fed’s Next Hike For the Fed, this clears the way for a hike. After last month’s hot inflation print put the next increase in ‘when’ not ‘if’ territory, a soft jobs report was the one thing that could have complicated December. If Fed hawks were waiting to exhale, they can do so now. CME FedWatch saw Fed hike odds increase, as anticipated. The 10-year yield edged up on the announcement, and yields and hike odds remain the two things to watch for mortgage rates. Midterms or Not, Housing Needs Real Wage Gains and Cooler Inflation One question that keeps coming up is whether the midterms changed anything for the housing market. In the short run, not much – the Iran War and its impact on inflation and mortgage rates remain the major wildcard. Getting back to “normal” in many metros takes more activity, which depends on improved buying power to bring buyers off the sidelines. Mortgage rates have declined for three straight weeks, to 7.18% , after a massive 74 basis point surge from late August to mid-October, but wages are the other half of buying power. That 3.1% annual wage growth is nominal, and it trails September’s 3.7% inflation and likely won’t keep up with where inflation is headed. Nominal wage growth is necessary but not sufficient for real wage gains in this environment, so inflation has to come back down too. A more dynamic labor market and cooling inflation are sorely needed for demand.

Units under construction totaled 18,068 units at quarter-end, with more than three-quarters of active development located in King County. Snohomish County rents declined slightly from a year ago but remained competitive at $2.23 psf. Regional rents have stayed above $2.50 psf since early 2024, supported by steady demand and improving occupancy fundamentals. With absorption continuing to outpace new deliveries and vacancy trending downward, conditions are becoming increasingly favorable for future rent growth. items.title: Inflation Persists in October
items.description: Inflation Persists in October November 10, 2026 Fan-Yu Kuo No Comments Inflation remained elevated in October even as energy prices eased, raising expectations of another Fed rate hike. Shelter returned as the largest driver of headline inflation, accounting for over 30% of the monthly increase. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy components, rose by 0.3% for the third consecutive month, suggesting broad-based price pressures across the economy. The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not release the annual inflation figure this month as October 2025 data is unavailable for comparison due to last year’s government shutdown. On a monthly basis, the CPI rose by 0.4% in October (seasonally adjusted), while the “core” CPI increased by 0.3%. The monthly increase in core CPI has remained at 0.3% since August. The price index for a broad set of energy sources increased by 0.7% in October, as decline in natural gas (-0.8%) was offset by increases in fuel oil (+2.0%), gasoline (+1.0%) and electricity (+0.9%). Meanwhile, the food at home and food away from home indexes rose by 0.4% and 0.5% respectively. Outside of energy, other top contributors that rose in October included indexes for recreation (+%), medical care (+0.3%), motor vehicle insurance (+0.7%), household furnishings and operations (+0.2%) and education (+0.3%). Meanwhile, the indexes for used cars and trucks (-1.2%) and communication (-0.1%) were among the major indexes that decreased over the month. The index for shelter, which makes up more than 40% of the “core” CPI, rose by 0.3% in October, following the same increase last month. The index for owners’ equivalent rent (OER) and rent of primary residence (RPR) increased by 0.3% and 0.2% over the month. NAHB constructs a “real” rent index to indicate whether inflation in rents is faster or slower than core inflation. It provides insight into the supply and demand conditions for rental housing. When inflation in rents is rising faster than core inflation, the real rent index rises and vice versa. The real rent index is calculated by dividing the price index for rent by the core CPI (to exclude the volatile food and energy components). In October, the Real Rent Index fell by 0.1%. items.title: October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices
items.description: October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices Published on November 10th, 2026 by Dana Anderson The median U.S. home-sale price fell in October for the first time in over 3 years. Prices are still rising rapidly in some metros with hot markets, including San Francisco, where they rose 16.8% year over year, and the greater New York City area. Home sales fell as mortgage rates surpassed 7%–but flattening prices could bring buyers a bit of relief. Would-be sellers are starting to pull back as demand declines, but the total number of homes for sale climbed to its highest level since 2020. For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended. The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year , even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023. With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices. Home Prices Are Still Rising Fast in Hot Markets, Led By San Francisco Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County. In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market. Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand . U.S. Pending Home Sales Drop to Lowest Level Since the Pandemic National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020. This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33% , a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before. All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here . “It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.” Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier. The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand . Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters. Housing Supply Builds to Highest Level Since 2020 With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025. More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage: Three in five homes are selling under asking price. 61% of homes that sold in October went for less than their original list price. More sellers are cutting their prices. 36% of homes that sold in October had at least one price drop–the highest share in our records. Roughly 15% of pending sales fell out of contract. That’s the highest share in our records other than the pandemic spike in March and April 2020. items.title: The Next Dollar: How Generational Spending Shifts Are Reshaping Retail Real Estate
items.description: The Next Dollar: How Generational Spending Shifts Are Reshaping Retail Real Estate Nov 10, 2026 U.S. Retail Research Report The next generation of retail growth is taking shape. Download Report Authors Nicole Larson Senior Manager, National Retail Research | U.S. Anjee Solanki National Director, Retail Services & Practice Groups The next generation of retail growth is taking shape. Who will drive the next dollar of retail spending, and what will it mean for physical stores? Colliers' latest retail report, The Next Dollar, explores how shifting consumer spending power, shopping behaviors and generational preferences are reshaping the retail landscape through 2030. While millennials will remain the largest consumer spending group, Gen Z is emerging as a major force in retail growth. At the same time, physical stores continue to play an essential role across all six generations, serving different needs for discovery, convenience, service and connection. Inside the report: A new generation of spending power: Gen Z spending is projected to grow 85.6% to $1.61 trillion by 2030, while Millennials retain the largest share of retail spending. The enduring value of physical retail: Every generation is expected to make the majority of its retail purchases in stores through 2030, reinforcing the importance of the physical shopping experience. The categories capturing growth: Foodservice, apparel and beauty are among the fastest-growing retail categories, creating opportunities for evolving tenant mixes and cross-shopping. The influence of tomorrow's consumers: Gen Z is driving demand for wellness, discovery and real-world connection, while Gen Alpha is already influencing household purchasing decisions. For retailers, property owners and investors, understanding these generational shifts will be critical to creating destinations that remain relevant as consumer expectations evolve. items.title: Hot inflation report puts Fed on track for December rate hike
items.description: Hot inflation report puts Fed on track for December rate hike By Kyle Campbell CloseText About Kyle twitter ByKyleCampbell Published November 10, 2026, 8:53 a.m. EST | Updated November 10, 2026, 9:38 a.m. EST 4 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh. Bloomberg News Key insight: The latest CPI inflation report, which showed inflation rising 0.4% in October, puts more pressure on the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates. Recent comments suggest policymakers will be ready to hike. Expert quote: " I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take." — Fed Gov. Christopher Waller Inflation rose faster than expected last month as lower energy costs could not offset broader price increases, according to Tuesday's consumer price index report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, rising 0.4% on the month. Processing Content The October CPI reading exceeded the consensus market forecast which expected a monthly increase of 0.24%. The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not issue an October CPI report last year, so the agency did not publish an annualized rate of inflation for last month. The print is better than September, when prices rose 0.6% month over month and 3.7% year over year, but hints at a troubling trend of accelerating inflation. Ahead of the report, Federal Open Market Committee members were already expressing increased concern about prices. Hours before the report was released, Fed Gov. Christopher Waller said his baseline expectation was that inflation would improve from September but the committee will still raise its benchmark interest rate a quarter percentage point next month. Even if inflation had come in below 0.3%, Waller said in a pre-written speech delivered in London, he would have backed a 25 basis point hike. With the October reading coming in above that level, he could support a bigger increase. "I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points at the FOMC's December meeting," Waller said. "That's my plan if things proceed as I expect. But if the October CPI inflation data out later today are similar to the past two monthly readings … then a stronger policy move may be needed. In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take." Waller joined the majority of FOMC voters in supporting their move to keep interest rates unchanged during the committee's meeting last month. In his speech he said this was appropriate because the group had already clearly signaled its intent to raise rates repeatedly, enabling market participants to price such a change into their valuation models. Yet, while the committee bought itself some flexibility in September, Waller said it must follow through on this "sooner rather than later" or else risk losing the trust of financial markets. Read more: OCC: Banks need strong controls when delegating to AI agents Democratic wave gives state AGs more enforcement sway Midterm drubbing may complicate GOP lame duck priorities FDIC taking more piecemeal approach to bank failures Inflation has been the FOMC's primary concern for months, as price growth from supply-side shocks — including tariffs and the war in Iran — have proven to be persistent. Meanwhile, the Fed's other top priority, maintaining maximum employment, has been firmly in hand. The U.S. economy added 165,000 last month and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%. Waller is not the only Fed official who has called for tighter monetary policy. Two FOMC participants voted against last month's policy hold, Fed Gov. Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack, both of whom preferred a hike. Cook has yet to explain her rationale. Hammack, in a speech delivered in Zurich, Switzerland last week, noted that inflation has been above the Fed's 2% target for nearly six years and has recently shown signs of broadening out beyond volatile food and energy prices. Because of this, she, too, anticipates monetary policy being tightened. "I expect that monetary policy will need to move to a restrictive stance to bring inflation back to 2% in a timely manner," Hammack said. "I prefer getting to that stance through more frequent smaller adjustments when possible, something which would be less disruptive to households, businesses, and financial markets." items.title: San Diego apartment supply is about to peak
items.description: San Diego apartment supply is about to peak by Kim O'Brien Posted November 5, 2026 in Insights San Diego apartment supply hit a record high in the past year and is set to peak in 1st quarter 2027. In the year-ending 3rd quarter 2026, roughly 6,600 units completed across San Diego, marking the highest annual total since Realpage Market Analytics began tracking the market in 2000. Supply in the past year also surpassed the market’s decade average around the 4,000-unit mark. Annual supply in San Diego is expected to remain elevated, peaking in the year-ending 1st quarter 2027, when roughly 6,880 units are scheduled for completion. After that, supply is slated to come down, aligning closer to the market’s decade average by the end of 2027. Demand is keeping pace with record apartment supply in San Diego, as evidenced by occupancy at 95.7% in October and rents up 1.5% year-over-year. After supply hits its peak and starts to come down, this market is projected to see improvement in both of those metrics. items.title: Mortgage rates ease as buyers gain leverage with concessions, ARMs
items.description: Mortgage rates eased slightly this week but stayed above 7.3%, keeping affordability tight and forcing loan officers to lean on seller concessions and adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) to close deals. At HousingWire ’s Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, 30-year fixed-rate mortgages averaged 7.35%, down from 7.38% one week earlier. Rates for 30-year jumbo loans averaged 7.56%, a 6-basis-point decline, while 30-year Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans were up 6 bps to 7.22%. “Since early October, rates have improved about 100 basis points, which can equate to an eighth of a point to 0.375, so that’s helping affordability," said Shannon Hoff, a California-based mortgage broker at Hoff Home Loans . Inflation remains a key obstacle. Data released Tuesday showed the Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% on a monthly basis in October, hotter than expected, keeping the door open for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its December meeting. “Because that’s creating uncertainty, I am seeing buyers are still extremely payment-sensitive,” Hoff said. “However, during the COVID-19 pandemic, people were having to pay $100,000 over for the listing price. If your payment is going to change $100 or $200 from where you want the rate to be, in the big picture, that's not so worrisome.” First American senior economist Sam Williamson said hotter inflation is likely to prolong the wait for real mortgage rate relief. “ Stronger job growth may give some households the income to move, but elevated borrowing costs raise the hurdle for everyone,” Williamson said in a statement. “Until mortgage rates ease, life moves will keep the housing market moving, while discretionary buyers wait on the sidelines.” In this context, Optimal Blue 's October 2026 Market Advantage mortgage data report showed that rate-lock volume fell 19% month over month and 38% year over year. But ARMs represented 17% of total lock volume, the highest share in the report going back to 2019. "ARM share reached another high, FHA gained share and first-time buyers took a larger share across the major agency programs," Brennan O'Connell , director of data solutions at Optimal Blue, said in a statement. "For lenders, that means the opportunity is increasingly in helping borrowers find the product and payment structure that works for their circumstances." Buyer's market? As fewer borrowers are able or willing to buy at today’s rates, inventory is starting to build in parts of the country. That's giving buyers more leverage, while pushing sellers and builders to participate more heavily in financing costs. That’s the opposite of a few years ago, when rock-bottom rates, intense competition and limited supply forced buyers to bid far above list price and waive contingencies. “I'm licensed in nine states, I get to see various markets, and a lot of them are leaning toward the buyer,” said Gay Veale , a 30-year U.S. Air Force veteran and owner of Guidon Mortgage Group . “Because of that, there’s often seller concessions involved, and I am seeing people use those seller concessions for as many different ways to do rate buydowns or get their mortgage to be cheaper in the beginning, at least, if possible.” Veale cited one deal in which a borrower received $58,000 in seller concessions — an unusually high figure — and locked a 6% rate. With a 3-2-1 temporary buydown, a permanent buydown and an adjustable-rate mortgage, the borrower’s effective initial rate fell to 2.75%. “Around 75% of my clients are getting seller concessions. They're not all that much, but at least $10,000 is an average for me,” Veale said. Needs-based buyers Veale said most buyers using ARMs today are opting for products that provide about five years of lower rates before they reset . That roughly matches borrower expectations that rates could ease somewhat over the medium term. She added that most of her current clients are “need-to-move” borrowers rather than investors , such as people relocating for a job, dealing with a death in the family, welcoming a new child or trying to get closer to relatives. Investment purchases are far less common than during the pandemic period, she said. Veale said her business volume this year looks very similar to last year, an outcome she called “very atypical of the market” and not something she expects to see again under normal conditions. In Northern California , Hoff said weaker demand is allowing some buyers to negotiate steep price cuts and substantial credits. She pointed to a client scheduled to sign on Wednesday for a new home after securing $50,000 off the purchase price and $10,000 in seller credits. That $60,000 swing would have been unattainable in a hotter market, she said. “That $60,000 is much more than paying a half of a point or a point higher in rate," she said. "Not only is it the uncertainty affecting the buyers, it's also affecting the sellers." Down payment dynamics have shifted as well. During the pandemic, borrowers using down payment assistance or putting 3% down struggled to compete with cash offers and large down payments. Today, Hoff said, these buyers are reappearing. She is seeing “more first-time homebuyers jump in the market with challenged credit, down payment assistance, outside-the-box loans, bank statements . My loans are definitely a lot more challenging now.” Related More: 30-Year Fixed Mortgage Adjustable-Rate Mortgage Mortgage Rates Center

items.title: Camden lowers guidance after September concession resurgence
items.description: Camden lowers guidance after September concession resurgence The REIT still saw improvement in expenses and new lease growth in Q3, though rising interest rates forced it to cancel property and land acquisitions. Published Nov. 6, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Wall Street sign with american flags and New York Stock Exchange in Manhattan, New York City, USA. Getty Images Camden’s Property Trust lowered its 2026 same-store revenue midpoint by 50 basis points to 0% after a weaker-than-expected September and the expectation of greater seasonal decline in the fourth quarter, according to the REIT’s executives on Friday’s third-quarter earnings call. Performance in September, specifically, surprised the company and set the stage for that revision, according to CEO Alex Jessett. “It was a greater decline in traffic than we had expected,” Jessett said. “And when we had the decline in traffic, obviously, you have to reduce your prices if you're trying to increase traffic.” Jessett said concessions, which were “incredibly sticky,” ranged from three weeks in West Palm Beach, Florida, up to two months in Austin, Texas, as merchant builders continued to offer steep discounts. “The third quarter, at least July and August, were so strong that we would have expected to see others start to dial back their concessions, and they absolutely did not do it,” Jessett said. Despite the September slowdown, there were positives: Camden expects same-store YOY expense growth of 1.75%, which is 75 bps better than the REIT’s prior midpoint and 125 bps better than beginning-of-year guidance, according to CFO Ben Fraker. The company was also “the only S&P 500 multifamily REIT to experience sequential improvement for both new lease rates and blended lease rates each quarter this year, and we were the only one with second- to third-quarter acceleration,” according to Jessett. Camden saw positive signs into Q4, though high-concession markets weighed on results. The REIT finalized its massive California sale and multiple acquisitions, though the interest rate environment forced it to cancel other deals. Rent trends Like many companies in supply heavy markets, Camden saw new leases remain in negative territory in Q3, falling to -2% YOY, according to its Q3 earnings release. In Q2, Camden’s new lease rate came in 130 bps lower at -3.3%. In Q3, renewals rose 3.6% YOY, giving the REIT a blended rate of 1%. In Q2, renewals increased 2.8% YOY and blends were -0.2%. “While renewal growth was in line with our expectations, new lease and blended lease growth were at the low end of our anticipated ranges, likely driven by the persistent concessions that remain in many of our core markets and sub-markets,” Camden Chief Operating Officer Laurie Baker said on the Q3 call. Camden sent out renewal offers to residents with December and January expirations at an average increase of 4.5%, according to Baker. That isn’t the only positive indicator. “We have seen signed new leases improve pretty dramatically in October as compared to September, and when we look at our October numbers and we compare them to October of last year, we're seeing really significant improvement,” Jessett said. Southeast Florida, at 1.6% YOY revenue growth; Atlanta, at 1.5%; Dallas, at 0.8%; and Houston, at 0.6%, were the top markets for Camden in Q3, according to a company Securities & Exchange Commission filing. Concessions have played a role in their performance, according to Baker. “We're seeing the strongest markets in Atlanta, Southeast Florida, Dallas and Houston,” Baker said. “And so, where those lower concessions are, we're obviously getting a little more pricing power, and we're having the ability to improve our occupancy.” On the other end of the spectrum were Denver, with a 5% YOY revenue decline; Nashville at -3.1%; Tampa, Florida, at -1.3%; and Orlando, Florida, at -0.7%, according to the SEC filing. “We still are continuing to see Denver and Nashville as those that have concessions that have been persistent,” Baker said. Buying and selling In July, Camden closed its sale of 11 properties with 3,620 apartment homes to a BlackRock-managed vehicle for $1.6 billion, recognizing a gain of $1 billion. The REIT used approximately $0.9 billion to retire balances outstanding under its unsecured revolving credit facility and commercial paper program, according to the Q3 earnings release. The REIT used $125 million to fund its August property and land acquisitions; $50 million to repurchase shares in August and early September; and $495 million toward the redemption of $500 million of senior notes due in November and to pay down borrowings in its commercial paper program. It had $55 million remaining in cash investment accounts for general corporate purposes, Fraker said on the call. In Q3, the REIT acquired Camden Brandon, a 296-unit property in Tampa; Camden LoSo, a 343-unit property in Charlotte, North Carolina; and Camden Gulch, a 300-unit property in Nashville, Tennessee, for a combined $305.2 million, according to the release. Camden acquired a land parcel in Tampa for approximately $18.3 million and sold 2.6 acres of land in Los Angeles for approximately $10.7 million, according to the release. Camden canceled the purchase of two properties and one land parcel in Q3 after interest rates rose , according to Jessett. “We went back looking for price adjustments, and clearly the sellers were not quite willing to capitulate to what we were looking for,” Jessett said. The REIT has also decided not to move forward with Nashville and Denver development projects at this time. items.title: UK Pension Funds Set For £340M BTR Buy
items.description: Pexels/Lennard A pair of UK pension funds are in talks to buy a £340M UK build-to-rent portfolio from a joint venture between the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and Greystar . Northern LGPS and Local Pensions Partnership Investments have teamed up for their second major rented residential acquisition, the Fizzy Living portfolio owned by the international JV, Green Street News reported . The portfolio comprises eight assets and 974 existing homes in and around London. It was one of the first BTR portfolios built in the UK. ADIA backed Thames Valley Housing in the creation of the portfolio, and Greystar bought out Thames Valley’s position in 2021. The pair appointed JLL to find a buyer earlier this year. At the end of last year, Northern and LPPI teamed up to take private PRS REIT , a single-family housing specialist, in a £1.1B deal. The company owns 5,478 homes, and the pair have created a housing investment platform called the UK Housing Partnership, run by Waypoint Asset Management, Green Street reported. When the Fizzy Living assets are added to that platform, Northern and LPPI will own 6,500 rental homes, making the partnership one of the biggest owners in the country, across two property types, urban BTR and single-family. Both investors are part of the tranche of newish pooled local government pension funds, which combined the assets and functions of myriad smaller local authority pension schemes. The aim is to mirror the sophistication and investment power of Canadian or Australian superannuation schemes. And these funds have been particularly interested in rented residential. Earlier this year, Border to Coast bought a £450M single-family-home portfolio from Blackstone ’s Leaf Living . items.title: Home trends you’ll see in 2027, according to Zillow
items.description: Home trends you’ll see in 2027, according to Zillow by Emily Marek November 10, 2026 Color drenching is likely to be one of the top home trends of 2027, with the keyword increasing 84% in listing descriptions on Zillow. (Image via Zillow) Quiet tech, elevated luxuries and color-drenched rooms will be among the most popular home trends in 2027, according to a new report from Zillow . The listing giant analyzed keywords in listing descriptions across its site to determine features that are increasingly desirable — and increasingly undesirable — to home shoppers. Since listing descriptions are a real-time indicator of how homes are being marketed, Zillow said, they offer a sneak peek of characteristics, designs and upgrades that are likely to take over home trends in the near future. With that in mind, here are the top home trends Zillow predicts for the upcoming year. Tech … and space to unplug from it While mentions of AI-powered appliances are up 119% year over year on Zillow, “spaces to unplug” have also jumped 34% as “digital detox” becomes an increasingly luxurious concept, said Zillow’s home trends expert, Amanda Pendleton. “Homes are getting smarter, but buyers also want tech-free zones where nothing needs charging. Sellers and their real estate agents are now highlighting spaces to unplug,” Pendleton said in a press release. “Taken together, this data suggests buyers value homes that are functional and efficient but still feel polished and personal.” ‘Elevated’ styling While listing descriptions show that buyers and homeowners still want their spaces to feel “cozy,” the up-and-coming trend is a more luxurious, polished feel. “Cozy” is still one of the most popular Zillow keywords, although mentions decreased 22% year over year, alongside words like “eclectic” (down 19%) and boho (down 13%). Instead, listings that mention “elevated” spaces and features increased 71%. Bold accents Specific trends within the elevated styling craze include color-drenched walls, which increased 84%; painted brick exteriors, which increased 27%; and board-and-batten walls and siding, which increased 24%. Efficiency Listings are now far less likely to mention sustainability features than they were over the past few years: Buzzwords like “sustainable” and “green” both fell 26% year over year. Instead, buyers now want to know that their home is efficient. Increasingly popular are behind-the-scenes features like fresh-air ventilation systems (up 52%), recirculating hot-water systems (up 52%), whole home batteries (up 43%), backup batteries (up 25%), air filtration (up 25%), water filtration (up 22%) and radon mitigation (up 18%). Multigenerational living spaces “ Multigenerational living ” is ever on the rise among today’s prospective homeowners, with the keyword jumping in popularity by 58%. Further indicators of the rise of multigenerational living — and the increasing age of today’s typical homeowner — include trending features like grab bars (up 18%) and wide doorways (up 13%). Less room for kitchens, more flexibility The prominence of chef’s kitchens and gourmet kitchens decreased by 21% and 15%, respectively, suggesting homeowners are willing to trade kitchen space for square footage elsewhere in the home. Meanwhile, mentions of home offices increased 42%, while media rooms rose 37% and flex spaces increased 35%. At the same time, mentions of open concept layouts remain steady. Modern wellness features Wellness features are still important, but not the same ones as years’ past. Cold plunges are decreasingly popular, with mentions falling 44%; similarly, mentions of Jacuzzis and jetted tubs decreased 9%. Instead, buyers are more interested in “spa-inspired” bathrooms, which increased in popularity by 60%. Exercise-related features like golf simulators (up 29%) and home gyms (up 18%) are also trending. Catios Feline friends deserve luxury spaces, too — and now they’re getting them, increasingly more than their canine counterparts. Dog grooming stations fell 16% on Zillow, while mentions of dog parks were stagnant. Instead, catios — screened-in outdoor areas for cats — increased 32%. items.title: This Dallas Startup Raised $4 Million to Expand Children's Access to Mental Healthcare
items.description: Live Poll Dallas-based Triplemoon has raised $4 million to expand its seed funding to $7.5 million. Founded in 2023, the startup works with pediatricians and family doctors to make mental healthcare part of children’s routine medical care. So far, the company’s footprint includes Texas, California, Tennessee, Florida, Maryland, Virginia, Connecticut, and Washington, D.C. In the Lone Star State, Triplemoon is partnered with 30 providers. This round, co-led by LiveOak Ventures and Activate Venture Partners, prepares the company for its next phase of growth. In an exclusive interview with D CEO, founder and CEO Lauren Gage shared how the latest round will scale Triplemoon’s current capabilities, how the company has transformed since its establishment in 2023, and how a team of medical experts is creating more accessible healthcare for today’s youth. Introducing: The POWER 50 Our new program spotlights North Texas executives under 50 shaping the region’s future. Nominations are open through Nov. 13. Learn More Meet the Team Behind Triplemoon “I don’t think anyone grows up thinking, ‘When I’m older, I’m going to work in mental healthcare.’ All of us who are working in mental health services got here through some type of lived experience,” Gage told D CEO . Her moment of inspiration was two-fold. After personally supporting a family member through mental health challenges and becoming a parent herself, Gage’s perspective shifted when she saw firsthand the gap in access to necessary behavioral health resources. “It was a moment I had in my own pediatrician’s office with my daughter when she was 6 months old that helped me realize what was going on in my life,” she says. “It was that experience that catapulted me into the journey I’m on.” After her own experience in the pediatric health space following the birth of her daughter, Lauren Gage (left) was inspired to establish health tech company Triplemoon. Triplemoon While Gage doesn’t have a formal medical background, she has a business acumen developed from her work at Goldman Sachs and McKinsey & Co. and rooted in her education from the University of Michigan and Duke University. “Working with consumer product companies helped me understand the customer experience and how important it is to understand the way a customer—or, in our case, a patient—experiences the service you offer,” she told D CEO. “ Combined with my lived experience in mental health, that helped to create the Triplemoon that we are today.” To support the company’s evidence-based work, Gage assembled a lineup of experts to direct and guide Triplemoon. This includes support from a clinical team of 20 licensed industry experts and chief clinical officer Dr. Katie Sardone, who’s been with Gage since the initial seed round wrapped in May 2025. “She’s worked in a lot of academic institutions and integrated primary care centers. She’s the perfect yin to my yang, if you will, of the business and the clinical side of things.” Another healthcare pro lending some hands-on support is board-certified internist and psychiatrist Dr. Caroline Carney, CEO of national behavioral health company Magellan Health and chief medical director at Heart City Health. “She really gets in the weeds with us and provides great direction,” Gage says. “We problem-solve some things you would think a board member never gets involved with.“ Integrated Treatment Strategy To minimize barriers to access for families in need of behavioral health services and offer additional resources for primary care providers, Triplemoon provides virtual mental health services under a primary care medical code, lowering costs for patients and allowing clinics to seek appropriate reimbursements for their services. “As an organization, we are providing behavioral health intervention, medication support to the provider, care coordination, going into schools, working with downstream subspecialties, and educating the families. And we’re doing all of that with patients on a day-to-day basis and also making sure our primary care partners are in the loop,” Gage said. The coding also makes these resources more readily available for those on Medicaid in addition to patients on commercially available insurance, an important consideration for Gage in the company’s early stages that also informed its expansion strategy. “One of the best parts about this model–and I think this is especially relevant to the population of Texas–is that it provides unprecedented access, not only for those of us living in the Dallas Fort Worth area, but also to patients living in more remote areas,” she told D CEO. “Especially in a state like Texas, where we have a pretty substantial population that lives in areas that are hours away from major health systems and more advanced mental health resources, having Triplemoon integrated into their primary care pediatric clinic could be a game changer for families in those communities.” Where the Dallas Company Is Headed Next Gage shared that the company plans to invest in its Texas, California, Florida, and Maryland markets over the next year to build and strengthen relationships with pediatric clinics and continue refining the clinical and technical product needed to keep these resources available to families. items.title: Hot Inflation Report and Hawkish Comments From Fed’s Waller Put a 50 Bps December Hike in Play
items.description: Hot Inflation Report and Hawkish Comments From Fed’s Waller Put a 50 Bps December Hike in Play Published on November 10th, 2026 by Chen Zhao Takeaway: A hot inflation report coupled with aggressive remarks from Fed Governor Waller overnight locks in a December rate hike and brings up the possibility of a larger 50 bps hike or a previously unanticipated hike in January. Core CPI, which excludes energy and food, came in at 0.296% month-over-month in October, down from the previous month, but higher than the forecasted 0.22%. Overall CPI came in at 0.350% month-over-month, also higher than the forecasted 0.25%. The inflationary pressure appears to be broad-based in this report, not coming from any single outlier category. Though there might be a small boost because of a distortion in how the Bureau of Labor Statistics seasonally adjusts this data after the government shutdown last year. Today’s data means the December 9th rate hike, which has been priced in, is definitely going to happen. The question now is whether they go 25 bps or a larger than usual 50 bps. Overnight Fed Governor Christopher Waller gave a speech in London saying “ But if the October CPI inflation data … are similar to the past two monthly readings—with core CPI inflation around 0.3 percent or even higher—then a stronger policy move may be needed. In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take. ” Lots of other Fed officials are on the calendar to speak later this week. The question now is whether they also support a 50 bps hike or if they would prefer to put a previously unanticipated January hike on the table instead. The latter may be preferable because going 50 bps after skipping a hike at the October meeting may look unusual. Chen Zhao Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics. items.title: Consumer Credit Growth Picks Up in the Third Quarter of 2026
items.description: Consumer Credit Growth Picks Up in the Third Quarter of 2026 November 10, 2026 Onnah Dereski No Comments Consumer credit growth accelerated in the third quarter of 2026, with both revolving and nonrevolving credit increasing at their fastest quarterly rates since 2022. Total outstanding consumer credit reached $5.22 trillion, continuing an upward trend that has strengthened over the past year. The acceleration comes amid elevated borrowing costs, although interest rates on both auto loans and credit cards continue to edge lower. According to the Federal Reserve’s G.19 Consumer Credit Report , total outstanding U.S. consumer credit reached $5.22 trillion in the third quarter of 2026. This marked a 4.21% increase at a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) from the second quarter, the highest quarterly increase since 2022. Compared to a year ago, total outstanding credit increased 3.01%, the highest growth rate in three years. Nonrevolving Credit Nonrevolving credit, which is primarily made up of student and auto loans (the G.19 report excludes mortgage loans), reached $3.86 trillion (SA) in the third quarter of 2026. This marks a 4.22% increase (SAAR) from the previous quarter, the highest quarterly increase since 2022. Additionally, nonrevolving credit rose 2.57% compared to one year ago, continuing the upward trend over the last five quarters. Student loans make up the largest share of nonrevolving credit, accounting for 49% of the total. In the third quarter of 2026, outstanding student loan credit reached $1.88 trillion (NSA), up 2.81% from a year earlier. The other large component of nonrevolving credit is auto loans. Auto loans reached a level of $1.59 trillion (NSA), showing a year-over-year increase of 1.89%, the largest increase in the last ten quarters. Auto loan rates for a 60-month new car stood at 7.54% (NSA) for the third quarter of 2026, 10 basis points lower than a year ago. Auto loan rates have continued to decline year-over-year for the last eight quarters but remain higher than pre-pandemic levels. Revolving Credit Revolving credit, which is primarily made up of credit card balances, rose to $1.37 trillion (SA) in the third quarter of 2026. This represents a 4.21% increase (SAAR) from the previous quarter and a 4.25% increase year-over-year. Although credit card rates have hovered near historic highs since Q4 2022, they have shown modest year-over-year declines over the past seven quarters. items.title: ARMs hit record 17% of locks: Pitch beyond the 30-year
items.description: ARMs hit record 17% of locks: Pitch beyond the 30-year By Spencer Lee CloseText About Spencer twitter Spencer_NYC linkedin spencer-lee-journo Published November 10, 2026, 1:57 p.m. EST | Updated November 10, 2026, 2:06 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email What's at Stake: Homebuyers seeking immediate affordability relief who risk facing severe sticker shock. Expert Quote: "October's data show how much affordability is shaping the purchase market." — Brennan O'Connell, Director of Data Solutions, Optimal Blue Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. A growing share of borrowers flocked to adjustable-rate mortgages in October, providing clues about where business may lie as well as the impact that the current economic environment is having on consumer behavior. The share of adjustable-rate mortgage locks last month hit 17%, the highest since the data was first tracked in 2019, according to Optimal Blue's Market Advantage Report. The ARM portion of locks rose from 14% one month earlier. Processing Content The new high mark came at the same time total rate-lock volume tumbled 19% from September and 38% on a year-over-year basis, with numbers falling across all loan categories amid ongoing macroeconomic pressures . Purchase lock volume decreased to an 84% share, relative to total activity, with demand slipping 18% and 17% from the prior month and year. The downward pressure across loan types led Optimal Blue's market volume index to plummet to a reading of 77 compared to 94 in September. "October's data show how much affordability is shaping the purchase market," said Brennan O'Connell, director of data solutions at Optimal Blue, in a press release. In other data showing the momentum currently boosting ARMs, the Mortgage Bankers Association reported lenders expanded availability of such financing for borrowers, especially those with lower loan-to-value ratios compared with recent history. The offerings helped push MBA's Mortgage Credit Availability Index higher for the first time in three months. The trends suggest that opportunities in today's subdued housing market exist outside the standard fixed-rate loan as long as originators can work with borrowers to find solutions that fit individual needs. ARM originations have historically risen when fixed rates surge, providing buyers with affordability relief for at least the first few years of their mortgage. The loans come with an initial fixed interest rate lower than the 30-year average. "For lenders, that means the opportunity is increasingly in helping borrowers find the product and payment structure that works for their circumstances," O'Connell said. Supporting its findings, Optimal Blue pointed out Federal Housing Administration-backed loans also accounted for an expanding percentage of mortgage locks, and first-time homebuyers grew in the agency market. The FHA segment made up 20% of locks, while Department of Veterans Affairs-backed mortgages took an 11% share, both up from September. Meanwhile, conforming loans made up 46% of all October locks, while non-conforming transactions accounted for 22%, both declining from the prior month. First-time buyers nabbed 45% of conforming purchase locks, climbing from both the previous month and year. Non-qualified mortgages, which are also experiencing heightened demand this year, made up 12% of October loan production, edging down from September but up by 195 basis points over the past three months and 420 basis points year over year. Non-QM lock volume split in close-to-equivalent shares between debt service coverage ratio, bank-statement and expanded guideline programs. Mortgage lenders see expanded credit availability The MBA's credit index increased 0.4% between September and October to a reading of 107.5, in part due to elevated ARM interest, with higher marks indicative of a greater number of products. In September, the MCAI settled at a score of 107.1, with a benchmark of 100 representing credit availability in March 2012, following the Great Recession. Unlike Optimal Blue's findings, though, government-product availability flattened, while conventional offerings grew, MBA reported. The uptick in ARM loans with lower LTV ratios included cash-out refinancing products, according to the trade association. "This also boosted the jumbo index, which was up to its highest level in three months," said Joel Kan, MBA vice president and deputy chief economist. The conventional MCAI increased 0.6%, while the government index grew by just 0.1%. Subindices within the conventional component showed jumbo offerings up 0.8% month to month and conforming credit unchanged. Look out for ARM regret Although lenders will appreciate the activity boosting their bottom line, recent history suggests consumers may want to approach them with caution. Research conducted in 2024 found approximately 70% of ARM borrowers expressed regret about their choice , with some facing sticker shock when the initial fixed term ended. Wacker, Chicago CHICAGO -- Cushman & Wakefield (NYSE: CWK), a leading global real estate services firm, today announced the sale of 121 W. Wacker, a landmark 41-story office tower overlooking the Chicago River and located at the gateway to Chicago's historic LaSalle Street corridor. The 441,030-square-foot property was acquired by two Chicago-based investors Ken Buckman and Robert Castillo, who intend to invest substantial capital to re-energize the nearly century-old building. Cushman & Wakefield's Cody Hundertmark and Tom Sitz represented the seller, Chicago-based real estate firm Ameritus, in the transaction. Following the acquisition, Cushman & Wakefield has been retained as the exclusive leasing agent for the property, with Mason Taylor and Paige Krueger leading leasing efforts. Unlike many institutional office investors, the principals come from business entrepreneurship and private equity. Their vision for the property's next chapter centers on long-term ownership, thoughtful modernization and renewing its prominence as one of downtown Chicago's enduring architectural landmarks. "Owning 121 W. Wacker is about much more than acquiring a real estate asset," said Buckman. "As Chicago residents, we felt strongly that 121 W. Wacker should remain in local hands. The property has a remarkable history, an irreplaceable location and a presence in the Chicago skyline that deserves thoughtful stewardship. We have ambitious plans to modernize the tenant experience while preserving the character and architectural details that make this one of the city's great buildings." The ownership group is planning a series of capital improvements to position the tower for the needs of today's leading companies. Enhancements include a significant upgrade to the outdoor amenity terrace and 24th floor conference center, a completely remodeled restaurant and bar managed by a leading Chicago hospitality firm and a refreshed main lobby experience. Award-winning international design firm Ware Malcomb will oversee all interior and exterior architecture, with Ameritus continuing as the building's property manager. Situated at the intersection of Wacker Drive and LaSalle Street, the property offers sweeping views of the Chicago River and skyline, immediate access to the Chicago Riverwalk and multiple public transportation options. The location places it amid the growing residential and business activity reshaping the Loop, just one block from Google's new Chicago headquarters, scheduled to open next year. "121 W. Wacker remains one of the most distinctive office buildings in downtown Chicago, offering something that cannot be replicated: authentic architectural character in an unmatched riverfront location," said Mason Taylor, Executive Managing Director, Agency Leasing at Cushman & Wakefield. "The new ownership group brings an entrepreneurial mindset, a genuine commitment to Chicago and a willingness to invest in the building's future. With planned upgrades throughout the property, it is exceptionally well-positioned to attract companies seeking a premier office environment, centrally located along Wacker Drive." Completed in 1930 and designed by renowned Chicago architects Holabird & Root, 121 W. Wacker stands as one of the city's most recognizable Art Deco skyscrapers. Originally known as the LaSalle-Wacker Building, the tower helped establish the northern gateway to Chicago's historic financial district and was among the last major buildings constructed in the city before the Great Depression. Now included within the West Loop-LaSalle Street Historic District on the National Register of Historic Places, the building has witnessed nearly a century of Chicago's evolution, with early ties to two iconic companies, United Airlines and McDonald's, both of which once maintained offices at the property. items.title: Sunlight, Weather and Childcare: A Year of New Data on Redfin Home Listings
items.description: Sunlight, Weather and Childcare: A Year of New Data on Redfin Home Listings Published on November 9th, 2026 by Isabelle Novak In 2026, Redfin added information about sunlight, weather, childcare access and more to home listings. Here is everything you need to know about what’s new. A home listing has always been good at telling you about a house: the square footage, the year it was built, the number of bedrooms. Historically, it has been less good at telling you what living there is actually like. Does the kitchen get morning sunlight? How hot are the summers? Is there a daycare within walking distance? Those are the questions we set out to answer this year. Multiple new data sets arrived on Redfin in 2026, and they now sit alongside other information that was already there, including scores about a property’s walkability, transit access and climate. Sunscore shows exactly how much sunlight a home gets Natural light is one of the hardest things to judge from listing photos or a single showing, and it matters more than you might expect. In a recent Redfin survey , nearly 70% of people said the amount of sunlight in their home affects their satisfaction with where they live, and 11% said it is non-negotiable when searching for a home. Sunscore is a property-level rating from 0 to 100 that shows how much sunlight a home gets. We co-created it with Shadowmap , a sunlight analysis platform, using 3D modeling that tracks how shadows fall across a home throughout the day and across the seasons. Here are the score breakdowns: ☀️ 0-50: Low sunlight ☀️ 50-70: Moderate sunlight ☀️ 70-80: Good sunlight ☀️ 80-90: Very good sunlight ☀️ 90-100: Exceptional sunlight Each score accounts for the home’s 3D shape and structure, surrounding buildings, trees and terrain, the sun’s position throughout the day, and seasonal changes across the year. In other words, it catches the things you would only discover after moving in—like a neighboring building that blocks the afternoon light in winter. And it is not only about comfort and aesthetics. A home’s sun exposure also says something about its solar potential, which can translate into real savings on energy costs over time. Weather data helps predict precipitation and heat Weather turns out to be one of the biggest reasons people move. In a recent Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos, 22% of Americans planning to move to another state said better weather was motivating the move—the most cited reason out of nearly 30 options, ahead of affordability, job opportunities and moving closer to family. Another 21% said concerns about climate change or natural disasters were shaping where they wanted to live. In July, we partnered with The Weather Company , owner of The Weather Channel app and weather.com, to bring historical weather data to every for-sale listing on Redfin. As our exclusive historical weather provider, it supplies the same data hundreds of millions of people check every month. Each listing shows ZIP code-level averages for: Temperature Precipitation Snowfall Humidity UV index Consider this information the difference between the weather on the day you tour a home and the climate you might actually live in. Childcare data displays daycare and preschool options For families with young children, childcare access can determine a neighborhood’s fit as much as school boundaries do. However, it’s historically been missing from the home browsing experience. Redfin is the first major real estate portal to partner with Winnie , the largest marketplace for childcare and early education in the U.S., to bring local childcare information to for-s a le listings. Nearby daycare and preschool options now appear on for-sale home listings with details that determine whether a spot is realistic for your family, such as: Distance from the home Tuition Licensing status Financial aid availability Staff certifications Location scores capture everything from wellness access to noise While Walk Score, Bike Score and Transit Score already existed on home listings, Redfin has expanded these location scores to capture more information about a neighborhood’s vibe using Local Logic data. Quiet Score: Level of noise nearby Wellness Score: Quantity of amenities within walking distance that cater to physical activity and healthy eating Vibrancy Score: Level of street activity nearby Start exploring homes on Redfin.com or the Redfin app to learn everything you’d want to know about a property. items.description: October Job Growth Beats Expectations, Keeping a December Fed Hike on the Table Published on November 6th, 2026 by Chen Zhao Takeaway: A strong jobs report gives the Fed permission to hike again in December should they want to. This morning’s data shows that 165,000 jobs were created in October and 84,000 more jobs were created in August and September than previously reported. That brings the six-month moving average of job creation to 83,000 jobs per month after briefly dipping into negative territory last fall. The professional and business services sector saw outsized gains with 70,000 jobs created in October, the strongest month in four years. If this doesn’t get revised away in coming months, it would be a significant data point to counter AI-related labor market anxiety. The unemployment rate ticked down very slightly by 0.03 pp to 4.14%. It had gotten as high as 4.5% last November before gradually drifting down. At this point, despite all the wild month-to-month swings after the BLS updated their methodology, it’s pretty clear the labor market strengthened meaningfully as the year went on. In recent months, the Fed has not been making their policy decisions based on the jobs report because they’re more worried about the inflation side of their mandate than unemployment. Today’s data allows them to continue that stance. Regarding the December 9th meeting, a hike is already mostly priced in. There’s still next Tuesday’s inflation data and one more jobs report before the meeting, but given the recent commentary from officials, a hike seems pretty likely. Chen Zhao Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics. items.title: A Looming Nor’easter Threatens Millions of Homeowners With First Snow of the Season
items.description: A potential nor’easter impacting the Northeast and New England is being forecasted for later this week, with millions of homeowners bracing for possibly the first snow of the season. Meteorologists are predicting that as early as Wednesday evening, a deep plunge in temperatures combined with a low pressure system moving across the Midwest will make for wet conditions for Louisville, KY , all the way up to Maine . While snow in these areas this time of year is not unheard of, some locales are prepping for a volatile winter ahead, given the Super El Niño conditions. So is this just a taste of what’s to come? A nor’easter in November Cold air sweeps across the East late in the week, setting the stage for winter weather, according to The Weather Channel . By Thursday night, a secondary low-pressure system is expected to form off the Eastern Seaboard. As cold air filters in, rain could begin mixing with or fully changing over to wet snow across interior parts of the Northeast. Friday into the weekend presents the greatest potential for snow, depending on the storm’s exact track, which meteorologists are still unclear on. If the system tracks close to the coast, it could wrap heavy inland snowfall into the Northeast alongside coastal rain, strong winds, and flooding. A track farther out to sea would result in much lighter snow accumulations across inland areas. Homeowners in places like Buffalo, NY , and Burlington, VT , are among those who should prepare for the snow shovels and salt for a snowy weekend. However, if the temperatures dip low enough, it wouldn’t be unthinkable to see snow in places like Washington, DC, Philadelphia, and New York City as well. Loading... Cold air will settle in for millions across the East as a storm could bring rain, snow, and winds to the Northeast. The Weather Channel Prepping for the winter Speaking of New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced ahead of the nor’easter a citywide mobilization to prepare Manhattan for winter weather. This includes a $25 million investment in an expanded Code Blue system and a supercharged snow- and ice-clearing operation. “We have spent the past year preparing for any challenge winter throws our way. We have trained our workers, readied our equipment and strengthened our protocols because keeping New Yorkers safe can’t begin when the first storm hits,” Mamdani said in a press release. “This winter, we’re doing things differently—we’re expanding Code Blue to reach more New Yorkers in need, equipping New York’s Strongest to clear snow and ice faster and leaving no stone unturned when it comes to protecting our neighbors from the cold. No New Yorker should face the dangers of winter alone, and no part of our city should be left behind.” These initiatives come at a time where New York and much of the surrounding states are bracing themselves for the final months of the Super El Nino, which, according to the latest forecasts from the World Meteorological Organization, is projected to be the strongest on record and likely to persist through February 2027. According to the NOAA , an El Niño system tends to be strongest during the winter months. But because of the strength of the system being tracked this year, there are plenty of variables at play. “Every El Niño is not the same; each one is unique with its own imprint on our weather,” says Ken Graham , director of NOAA’s National Weather Service (NWS). "Advanced monitoring and an improved understanding of El Niño patterns allow the NWS to better predict and better prepare the public and our core partners for what is to come.” With that in mind, the Farmers' Almanac 2026–'27 winter outlook outlines a season defined by sharp contrasts and volatile conditions across the United States, driven largely by an active El Niño pattern. In the Northeast, it predicts a season dominated by wet conditions, both rainy and snowy. In fact, much of the country will need to contend with wetter than usual conditions, but whether snow develops will depend largely on the temperatures. items.title: U.S. job gains bounce back in October
items.description: U.S. job gains bounce back in October by Chuck Ehmann Posted November 6, 2026 in Insights The U.S. labor market came roaring back in October after September’s initial estimated gain of 29,000 new jobs with a reported increase of 165,000 jobs for the month, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Revisions to the August and September numbers boosted previous estimates by a combined 84,000 additional jobs, bringing the year-to-date total through October to 861,000 jobs gained compared to 116,000 total jobs added in all of 2025. Industry gains were led by Professional/Business Services (+70,000 jobs), Education/Health Services (+53,000 jobs), Trade/Transportation/Utilities (+22,000 jobs), and Manufacturing (+19,000 jobs). Particularly strong subsectors include temp services, management and consulting, social assistance, hospitals, couriers and messengers, warehouse clubs, and computer and electronic manufacturing. The remaining industries experienced modest gains or moderate shortfalls. Losses were especially deep in Leisure/Hospitality Services (-13,000 jobs) with much of that decline in food services and drinking places (-7,200 jobs). Meanwhile, the U3 seasonally adjusted headline unemployment rate (from the survey of households) decreased slightly to 4.1% in October, remaining in a narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March. This post is part of a series analyzing employment data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. For more on this data, read previous posts on Job Growth .
