items.title: Power Scarcity Poses Problems For Charlotte Industrial Developers
items.description: Industrial developers in Charlotte are vying for power. Small-bay industrial projects and some build-to-suit sites in the region are competing for energy against data centers, large advanced manufacturers and other big power users, panelists said at Bisnow ’s Charlotte State of the Market event . But demand is surpassing availability. “There’s a lot of users that need smaller buildings that still have an amazing power demand,” Kirk Matthews, vice president for Frampton Construction, said at the event, held at The Westin Charlotte. “We’re seeing small product … 100K [SF], 150K [SF] that still need 10 megawatts, and they’re not data centers.” Unsplash/American Public Power Association Duke Energy , the primary power supplier in the Carolinas, predicted last year that through 2040, electricity demand across its two Carolina systems would rise 16% to nearly 60%, according to a report from the North Carolina Energy Policy Task Force. The increased demand stems from a surge in population growth in Charlotte, which added more than 20,000 people last year and is nearing 1 million residents. The region’s energy grid is aging but is taking on additional load growth as the data center boom continues, Axios reported . That demand could delay or cancel projects as regulators weigh how to balance energy needs, panelists said. “Our electrical grid is nowhere near what it needs to be,” Alan Lewis, managing partner at The Keith Corp., said at the Sept. 30 event. Unsplash/Winston Chen The rise in data center development across the U.S. is driving electricity demand, which is expected to more than double from 31 gigawatts in 2025 to 66 GW by 2027, according to Goldman Sachs Commodities Research. Access to power is becoming a key driver of where companies decide to build capital-intensive real estate projects in the U.S. Charlotte's industrial market faces other hurdles, including skyrocketing costs of materials like steel and concrete. But panelists cited power constraints as the most imminent problem. “It's everything,” Lewis said. “I mean, No. 1 on the list almost every single time is, ‘How much power do you have?’” Data Center Construction Is 'A Big Drain' Charlotte’s industrial market is experiencing strong leasing activity and stable rent growth, according to a CBRE report from the third quarter. The metro “remains attractive for industrial expansion,” with leasing activity at 3.2M SF, up 55.6% from the same period in 2025. Vacancy in the third quarter was 7.1%, down from 7.9% the previous year. But power availability is a primary challenge for the growing market. A single hyperscale data center facility can consume 20 MW to more than 100 MW of power, equal to powering 15,000 to 75,000 homes, according to IAEI Magazine . More than 100 data centers are operational across North Carolina, with around 40 of them in Charlotte, according to Data Center Map . Last month, Charlotte extended its 150-day moratorium on data center development by 11 months to give the city more time to develop policies and regulations around the digital infrastructure. Key concerns among data center opponents include power demands and rising utility costs. But data centers aren’t the only developments consuming energy from Charlotte’s grid. “The massive amount of data center construction, and all the reshoring and direct investment here in new industrial facilities, is a big drain,” Lewis said. He added that the mass conversion to electric vehicles in the area is putting even more “stress on the system.” At least one planned industrial project in the area was halted over electrical demands. In September, North Carolina regulators rejected Duke Energy’s proposal to build a $584M natural gas power plant near Hamlet that would generate about 255 MW by 2030, citing concerns over how residents would be protected from the project’s costs. “There are real challenges in accommodating the amount of demand for these larger, big investment-type projects that want to be in the Carolinas,” said Jordan Quinn, a partner at Trinity Capital Advisors who leads the firm’s industrial platform. Other industrial projects in the area are underway. Red Bull broke ground on a new $1.7B facility in Concord in September 2025, and Eli Lilly announced a $77M expansion to its manufacturing campus earlier this year. Allocating Megawatts Pexels/andres Nino Charlotte's skyline Charlotte’s small-bay development pipeline remains active, with approximately 1.5M SF expected to deliver this year and another 2.2M SF under construction, according to a Matthews report . These properties typically have an easier time securing power than larger sites due to their size limitations. But because of the increased energy demand, “the requirements for smaller manufacturers have just gotten more intense,” Lewis said. “Every park we have, every site we have, we try to get the best information we can on how much power we have available,” he said. When a developer plans to build out multiple buildings within an industrial park, it can be difficult to divide up megawatts. “You often find yourself saying, ‘Well, gosh, if I do this deal, I'm going to lose two-thirds of my power that I have for everything else,’” he said. Sometimes a site will end up requiring more power than developers initially predicted. In a 50K SF deal, a tenant may need 10K SF of office space for 50 people, Quinn said. Air-conditioning that space to bring those people in could require 10,000 amps of power. “It's just this incredible challenge as an owner of industrial real estate in the market to accommodate not only the tenants' needs but to get them in quickly, when [tenants] actually need the space,” Quinn said. “It's very, very, very tough.” Duke Energy executives are expecting a power surge next year, as 5.2 gigawatts for data centers will hit the grid beginning in the second half of 2027, according to The Charlotte Ledger . items.title: Why didn’t the strong jobs report send mortgage rates skyrocketing?
items.description: With all the crazy things happening this week, the blowout jobs report on Friday didn’t send mortgage rates up at all. But one thing is for sure: the labor market has been better in 2026 than it was in 2025. I once labelled the labor market the honey badger labor market and no matter what has been thrown at the U.S. economy after 2011 — outside the brief recession created by COVID-19 — the labor data has held up well. Let’s dig into why very strong jobs report didn’t push yields or mortgage rates higher, as we would normally expect with the Fed being so hawkish in their statement. From BLS : Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, and the unemployment rate changed little at 4.1 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment increased in professional and business services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. The labor data has improved enough that we have gone from a 4.5% unemployment rate last year to 4.1% today. Part of this is that labor-force growth has slowed and the break-even number has decreased, meaning fewer jobs are needed to keep the unemployment rate low. I have my break-even at 78,000 jobs created per month; I believe the Fed's is 33,000. Some economists have it at zero, which I think is silly. In any case, the unemployment rate is lower this year versus last year. Now, the low point in the COVID-19 recovery was about 3.4% unemployment back in 2023, so the unemployment rate has increased from that low, but it's still good enough to keep the Fed’s focus on inflation instead of labor. Jobs breakdown This month's report had growth in a few sectors, especially the business services sector jobs with one of the biggest monthly prints in years. There was also growth in manufacturing, and transportation & warehouse, while construction jobs faded a tad. Construction labor will be interesting in the future if mortgage rates stay elevated and short-term rates go up. If there is an AI slowdown and fewer AI data centers are being built, will this sector start to decline? One of my most critical recession indicators, residential construction employment, doesn’t look great lately, but it isn’t looking terrible either. In previous cycles, you can see a clear downtrend in this labor pool, which hasn’t happened in this cycle. With builders doing more rate buydowns — which have kept new home sales at 2019 levels over the past few years — and remodeling work holding up, this clear recession indicator hasn’t broken yet. 10-year yield and mortgage rates As crazy as this week has been, the jobs data wasn’t the big driver of mortgage rates as much as AI stock prices. CoreWeave's stock price was up 10% pre-market today, and bond yields ticked up with that. The jobs report didn’t do much to yields, we just saw a mild increase and then they fell back in line with the trend. Then CoreWeave stock price went almost negative, bond yields fell to the lows of the day, and now both have picked up from the lows! The market needs a weekend break. Mortgage rates ended the day flat at 7.17%, so as crazy as this sounds, the blowout jobs data didn’t send mortgage rates or bond yields much higher. That's good news for rates, and there are some levers the new Congress can pull to potentially get rates even lower, which I discussed on today's episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief Sarah Wheeler. Conclusion A lot has changed this week for the economy regarding the bond market and where mortgage rates can go. The blue wave has raised hopes that the trade war and the conflict with Iran can end soon, AI companies have shown they can bleed, and Congress will try to slow the AI boom as much as it can without crashing it. All these things happened this week, so that even with four solid jobs reports during jobs week, the 10-year yield closed at 4.86% and mortgage rates closed at weekly lows. Related More: Jobs Report

items.title: Opendoor says it's behind schedule but plans to catch up by 2027
items.description: Opendoor is behind schedule. Since taking over the company a little over a year ago, CEO Kaz Nejatian has promised that the firm would achieve adjusted net income positive status on a 12-month go-forward basis by the end of 2026. But the recent housing market downturn, triggered by the rapid rise in mortgage rates , has proven to be a bit of a roadblock. “We are currently behind but we intend to catch up,” the iBuyer’s third quarter 2026 earnings report explained. During the quarter, Opendoor recorded an adjusted net loss of $66 million and an actual net loss of $218 million, up from a $90 million net loss a year ago. This comes even as the company reported a 12% annual increase in revenue to $1.022 billion. “A year ago, I told you we would build a different Opendoor — faster, stronger, fully committed to our mission of tilting the world in favor of homeowners,” Nejatian said during his firm’s earnings call with investors and analysts on Thursday. “We have spent the past year building a machine, and that machine is getting better every single day. We are not done yet. It is not perfect, but it is getting better every single day. The question is this: Is Opendoor in a better economic condition than it was a year ago? The answer is obviously yes.” A more resilient Opendoor Nejatian’s confidence comes from his belief that Opendoor has become more resilient over the past year. This includes ways in which the company has worked to serve more sellers without adding more homes to the company’s balance sheet. “This past week, around half of the first offers our direct-to-consumer sellers accepted were listing or Cash Now, More Later. That lets us serve more sellers with less of our capital exposed to changes in the market,” Nejatian said. In the past 12 months, the company has done over $1 billion in Cash Now, More Later volume. “We have built more ways to meet sellers' needs and have made it easier for them to understand their options and make the choice they want for their own lives,” Nejatian said. “Sellers can now adjust the offer slides and make the choice that is good for their families.” Scaling without buying more homes? Nejatian noted that every other time Opendoor has tried to scale, it has done so by purchasing more properties, but that isn’t the case this time. “We proved that we can grow without buying growth. That's the single most important thing that has happened over the last year. We're changing that with our capital-light products,” Nejatian said. Still, Opendoor did purchase far more homes in Q3 2026 than it did in Q3 2025, with a 316% year-over-year increase to 4,865 homes. The company’s signed acquisition volume represented an estimated 0.56% of market share in the addressable U.S. market in Q3 2026 — more than four times higher than a year ago. On the sales side, Opendoor sold 2,728 homes, an increase of 160 homes compared to a year ago. At the end of the quarter, the iBuyer had 7,596 homes in its inventory, up from 3,139 homes a year ago. While the increase in inventory could be seen as cause for concern, especially heading into the slower winter housing market, Opendoor noted that homes listed for sale for 120 days represented just 18% of inventory at the end of the quarter, down from 50% a year ago. Despite the progress, Nejatian said the company still has work left to do on unit economics and resale velocity, something it needs to focus on as it strives for more resiliency. “We're not as good as we want to be, but we're in a much better place," he said. "When the market moves against you and you own homes, there's two things you can do. You can sell fast, or you can hold and wait and pray for the market to recover. We choose to clear. "The decline in late August and September knocked us off track on execution a little bit because we turned our attention to clearance rather than margin improvement. It costs something real in a quarter like this, but that's the right way to run this company for the long run.” To help with some of these challenges, Nejatian said Opendoor has turned to AI to help improve speed while still scaling. Some of these tools include an AI model that determines repair plans for every home to hit the market. The company said the system has been outperforming the old process of following a standard repair manual. Opendoor said it also built a system to help price homes. While humans still have final judgment, the software does the work of pulling applicable, comparable homes. Ancillary services and the future Nejatian also said that Opendoor is focusing on its mortgage division . In Q3, Opendoor said originations from its in-house lender were up 400% year over year. This comes as the iBuyer's lender is now licensed in 25 states, compared to none a year ago. In addition, the company also launched a beta test of Buy with Opendoor in the San Francisco Bay Area this week. The product allows the company to earn mortgage revenue on properties not affiliated with Opendoor in anyway. Looking to the future, Nejatian said Opendoor is hoping to build out title and escrow services — not only to add more efficiencies to Opendoor’s in-house transactions but to add additional revenue streams by serving consumers not in its ecosystem. “We need to grow, use less capital per transaction, and sell homes faster. Those are things we can control, and that is what we are focused on. What matters to us is solving the core problems of our business, and those are what we need to focus on,” Nejatian said. items.title: Zillow's agent tie-ins grab purchase share as market shrinks
items.description: Zillow's agent tie-ins grab purchase share as market shrinks By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published November 05, 2026, 4:39 p.m. EST | Updated November 05, 2026, 4:45 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Zillow's strategy of pairing its loan officers with invitation-only real estate agents is pulling purchase business away from the rest of the market. Its home loans unit grew purchase volume 55% in the third quarter while industry purchase originations fell. Processing Content Zillow Home Loans originated $1.972 billion of purchase loans in the third quarter, up from $1.276 billion a year earlier. Year-to-date volume is up 79%. Over the same quarter, Zillow estimates industry purchase origination volume declined 4%. "It's why purchase mortgage revenue for us is outgrowing the category even with the category declining," said CEO Jeremy Wacksman on the earnings call. The company is almost entirely a purchase lender. It did just $4 million of refinance production in the third quarter, versus $5 million one year prior. Second quarter volume was $2.181 billion, with only $7 million coming from refi. How the Preferred program feeds Zillow Home Loans The volume growth came as Zillow expanded the share of buyer connections sent through its Preferred program, an invitation-only network of real estate agents. Zillow previously called the program Flex. Executives reported double-digit adoption of Zillow Home Loans among customers working with Preferred agents. In Zillow's oldest markets, that rate is approximately 20%. "We are pleased that we continue to see double-digit customer adoption rates in Zillow Home Loans with our oldest markets at approximately 20% adoption rates, demonstrating that our integrated experience is adding value for both consumers and real estate agents," said Jeremy Hoffman, chief operating and chief financial officer. Wacksman framed the integrated model as the reason for Zillow's confidence in mortgage growth. "I mean 80% of buyers need both the mortgage and the agent. They want that as a one-stop shop," he said. "When we can offer that as an integrated experience, that's what they're choosing." He added that "a key part of this strategy is making sure that the Home Loans loan officer and the Preferred agent build a mutually beneficial relationship." The shift also changes how Zillow gets paid. Under its legacy advertising model, real estate agents used co-marketing dollars from lenders when bidding on leads, said Douglas Harter of BTIG. Under the Preferred model, Zillow captures mortgage revenue at origination, which can come six to 12 months later. Why mortgage revenue still missed The volume gains did not translate into the revenue analysts expected. Mortgage revenue rose 32% year-over-year to $70 million, but Keefe, Bruyette & Woods had forecast $81.3 million, putting the result 13.9% short. BTIG had forecast $81 million. Hoffman attributed the miss to " rate shock , which caused lower conversions." Industry purchase volume also came in weaker than Zillow planned for. "We estimate that industry mortgage purchase origination volumes were down 4% for Q3, below our expectation for a low-single-digit decline," he said. "We call out mortgage industry performance because the majority of Zillow buyers purchased their home with a mortgage." Harter tied the broader earnings miss to a weakening housing market and the "accelerated transition from the legacy ad model to Flex." Zillow underperformed existing home sales for the first time since the fourth quarter of 2024, which helped spread the miss into mortgage, he said in a research note. Zillow posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, compared with $10 million of net income in the third quarter of 2025. Zillow expects a steeper purchase decline in Q4 Zillow guided fourth quarter mortgage revenue to between $55 million and $56 million, with total revenue between $635 million and $665 million. "Our revenue outlook includes our expectation for a decline in year-over-year mortgage industry purchase origination volumes of 10% to 15%," Hoffman said. "This is down significantly from our prior industry expectation of mid-single-digits decline due to the sharp increase in mortgage rates we saw at the end of Q3 and into the start of Q4." Zillow expects 20% revenue growth in the fourth quarter as it scales outside its residential business, "with mortgage tailing off," Harter said. "The weakening housing market and bigger-than-anticipated model transition impact contributed to an 8-9% reduction in the 4Q revenue guide from the prior implied level," he said. items.title: NAR sees pent-up demand waiting on lower mortgage rates, better sentiment
items.description: The U.S. housing market is building “significant” pent-up demand that could be released if mortgage rates ease, inventory improves and consumer confidence rebounds, National Association of Realtors’ (NAR) chief economist Lawrence Yun told attendees Friday at NAR’s NXT in New Orleans. Yun contrasted today’s sales environmen t with the year 2000, noting that the U.S. population has grown from 281 million to 350 million and payroll jobs from 132 million to 159 million over that period. Housing wealth has ballooned from $7 trillion to $35 trillion, yet existing-home sales are tracking near 4 million this year , well below the 5.2 million homes sold in 2000, he said, citing NAR data. “Affordability is tough, but people’s incomes are rising, and if somehow mortgage rates go down, think about the potential housing demand that could be released to the marketplace,” Yun said. On the supply side, Yun said inventory has risen as sales have slowed. Months’ supply is now at its highest level since 2015, and the median home took 33 days to go from listing to contract in September, according to NAR. “Homes are staying on the market a little longer than before,” Yun said. “With longer days on market, you have to be realistic to the market condition. Otherwise, buyers will reject the homes on the market.” Yun pointed to consumer psychology as a key missing ingredient. Consumer sentiment has fallen to roughly half its 2000 level and is now worse than during the Great Recession, even as the labor market has added jobs. “If we can boost confidence levels, maybe that can also change the dynamics,” Yun said. First-time buyers remain near historic lows Jessica Lautz, NAR deputy chief economist and vice president of research, presented findings from the trade group’s newly released 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers . First-time buyers made up 22% of all buyers, near the series low, and the median age of first-time buyers held at a record-high 40. Those numbers underscore how younger households are delaying homeownership, even as they form households and enter peak earning years. For lenders and real estate brokerages, that means fewer entry-level transactions and more emphasis on move-up or equity-rich buyers. “ First-time home buyers are struggling,” Lautz said. “They’re not struggling just with housing affordability. They're also struggling with rent. They’re struggling with student loan debt, and a rising issue for first-time home buyers is childcare costs.” Lautz noted that sellers reported staying in their homes for a median of 12 years before selling, the longest tenure on record for the survey. “The golden handcuffs of low interest rate mortgages is true. People are holding on to those properties for longer periods of time,” she said. “It’s why we need to build more housing inventory—especially affordable housing inventory—for the potential first-time home buyers who are out there.” Agent usage hits record highs Despite technology and direct-to-consumer platforms, use of licensed professionals in transactions remained strong, according to NAR’s survey. A reported 90% of buyers purchased through an agent, the highest share in four decades, and a record 92% of sellers used an agent. “Sellers want agents to price that home competitively, find that qualified buyer, help with marketing, and make sure they get to the closing table in a time frame that they need to do so,” Lautz said. Why this matters for housing professionals For real estate agents and brokers, NAR’s data point to a market where transaction volume is constrained more by affordability, rates and sentiment than by underlying demand. A larger population, more jobs and higher housing wealth suggest that activity could accelerate quickly if mortgage rates retreat and confidence improves. For lenders, a 22% first-time buyer share and a median first-time buyer age of 40 highlight both near-term headwinds and an eventual backlog of delayed demand. Households that are renting longer and juggling student debt and childcare may respond strongly to any easing in rates, pricing or down payment constraints. For builders and developers, Lautz’s comments reinforce the policy and business case for adding affordable inventory . With existing owners locked in by sub-4% mortgages and staying put for a median 12 years, new construction remains one of the few levers to ease the entry-level shortage. Yun’s and Lautz’s remarks come as the industry also adjusts to p ost-settlement commission rule changes and elevated borrowing costs , making accurate pricing, counseling on affordability and clear communication with consumers more central to winning business in 2027 and beyond. A late-summer rise in delinquencies among mortgages backed by the government-sponsored enterprises points to an upward trend that may require servicers to keep resources available for agency loans until economic conditions improve. Processing Content Delinquency totals increased on a month-to-month basis across stages in August, according to data provided by the Federal Housing Finance Agency, the overseer of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. The number of borrowers 30 to 59 days delinquent climbed 6.9% to 313,254 from 292,965 between July and August . The number of mortgages past due by 60 days or more grew 2.9% to 256,999 units compared to 249,816 one month earlier. The representative share of delinquencies relative to all outstanding GSE-backed mortgages now stands at 1.03% for early-stage distress. Liens 60 to 90 days past due make up 0.84% of outstanding mortgages. Borrowers in serious delinquency or currently in foreclosure account for 0.6%. Although mortgage leaders in 2026 raised regular warnings about looming challenges for borrowers with Federal Housing Administration mortgages , the new data hints at difficulties surfacing in the agency segment. While distress eased in the early summer, delinquency volumes finished August higher than where they stood at the end of the first quarter, when they settled at 281,098 and 246,081, respectively. FHFA's findings suggest rising prices and economic uncertainty continue to take a significant toll on the ability of some homeowners to consistently meet monthly mortgage obligations, with downward pressure on affordability becoming more acute as 2026 progresses. The surge in summer delinquencies came at the same time prices of consumer goods ticked upward, with energy costs, in particular, accelerating from the impact of the Iran War. Meanwhile, the still-rising costs of property insurance and taxes are leading to prolonged sticker shock, even as the pace appears to be leveling off this year. Recent forecasts predict many of the same factors will weigh on affordability through next year. The extent of homeowner concerns showed up in the number of calls for legal assistance to deal with potential foreclosures in the late summer, which came in almost 15% higher at the end of the third quarter compared to a year ago. Lawyers at LegalShield specifically noted inflation's effect on household budgets as a primary cause , rather than poor planning on the part of borrowers. Foreclosure starts leap 18% FHFA's new report also found foreclosures on the rise among Fannie Mae- and Freddie Mac-backed loans. The number of foreclosure starts shot up 18% to 8,930 from 7,569 from July to August. Foreclosure and bank sales of properties eased 5%, though, to 1,333 from 1,403. A report from Auction.com saw such inventory likely to increase for the remainder of 2026, but much of the growth will be driven by FHA foreclosures. items.title: 5 Things We Learned From PwC And ULI's Emerging Trends 2027
items.description: Unsplash/Markus Spiske Europe's real estate market faces a volatile 2027. Europe’s property market is facing a longer and more uneven recovery than many investors had anticipated, with political uncertainty, higher financing costs and persistent economic headwinds continuing to hit confidence. But while the short-term outlook remains challenging, the latest Emerging Trends in Real Estate Europe 2027 report from PwC and the Urban Land Institute suggests that opportunities remain. Based on responses from 1,498 senior property professionals across Europe, the report highlights a shift in investment priorities. Rather than relying on broad market recovery, investors are increasingly focused on resilient income, operational improvements and individual assets with strong fundamentals. The report also identifies some of the structural forces reshaping the industry. Here are five key takeaways. 1. The recovery is taking longer than expected Just 45% of respondents expect business profitability to increase in 2027, down from 50% last year. Higher bond yields, inflation, construction costs and political uncertainty continue to weigh on the market. Investors are increasingly focused on resilient income and operational improvements. 2. London remains Europe's top investment destination The UK capital retains first place ahead of Madrid and Paris. Munich has climbed to fourth, overtaking Berlin, while Milan has risen two places to fifth. Amsterdam slipped one place to sixth, while Lisbon has entered the top 10, reflecting the growing appeal of southern European markets, and Dublin dropped a place to 14th. The report also highlights increasing interest in Warsaw as a major Central and Eastern European investment destination. 3. Data centres and energy infrastructure lead the pack Data centres rank first for investment prospects, followed by new energy infrastructure. Data centres also lead the rankings for investment, development and income growth by a significant margin, although concerns remain over the environmental impact of data centre development and the sustainability of artificial intelligence infrastructure spending. 4. Europe's housing crisis is an economic threat Affordability and supply constraints are now seen as the biggest challenges to Europe's long-term competitiveness, ahead of climate adaptation, infrastructure provision and social cohesion. Housing affordability ranks among the top three concerns for 34% of respondents. 5. Climate risk and AI are changing investment Some 59% of respondents expect physical climate adaptation to become a more pressing issue over the next five years, putting greater emphasis on building resilience and assessing climate risks before acquisitions. AI is also moving up the agenda, with 45% identifying it as a major issue for real estate over the next three to five years. While up just 1.3% from a year earlier, the amount is nearly 54% higher than in September 2019, according to NAR. The average rate on a typical 30-year fixed-rate mortgage is 7.3% as of Tuesday, according to Mortgage News Daily . "HELOCs let them borrow against their equity without giving up the low interest rate on their home," said certified financial planner Douglas Boneparth, president and founder of Bone Fide Wealth in New York City and a member of CNBC's Financial Advisor Council . Mortgage holders have $17.5 trillion in equity Mortgage holders collectively had $17.5 trillion in home equity as of the third quarter, according to a new report from Intercontinental Exchange, a financial markets technology and data company. Tappable equity that can be accessed — meaning a homeowner's equity would remain at or above 20% of the home's value after tapping it — rose 1.2%, or $16,600, from a year ago to an average of $204,000 per borrower, the ICE report shows. "Homeowners are sitting on substantial housing wealth, with 2.4 million mortgage holders now holding at least $1 million in equity," Andy Walden, head of mortgage and Housing Market Research at ICE, said in the report. Average HELOC rate is 7.49% HELOCs let you tap a line of credit over time as you need the money, instead of getting it all at once like a home equity loan or cash-out refinance. While HELOCs may have fewer upfront costs than a home equity loan, they generally have a variable interest rate. This means it will move up and down based on a benchmark like the prime rate, which banks use as a basis to set rates on a variety of loans. And, while the Federal Reserve doesn't control that rate, it is influenced by changes the Fed makes to the so-called federal funds rate. "If your budget only works at today's rate, then your budget doesn't really work," Boneparth said of HELOCs. "You kind of have to be mindful of the fact that rates may go up." If your budget only works at today's rate, then your budget doesn't really work. Douglas Boneparth President and founder of Bone Fide Wealth The average interest rate for a $30,000 HELOC was 7.49% as of Nov. 4, according to Bankrate . Many HELOCs also have a "draw" period when you can take money out, which often lasts five or 10 years. During that time, you typically are only required to pay the interest on any funds you've withdrawn. After that, however, you'll enter a repayment period of, say, 10 or 20 years, when you're required to pay both interest and principal. Because of that, your payments will jump if you've only been paying interest. "The real test comes when the repayment period kicks in, and the principal starts to show up, if that's how their HELOC is structured," Boneparth said. "Borrowing against your house to pay off credit cards is a little trickier because you're turning unsecured debt into debt secured by the roof over your head." items.title: Former Trump Admin Officials Raise $130M For Modular Data Center Startup
items.description: Just months after being founded by three former Trump administration officials, modular data center startup Mavria has already reached a billion-dollar valuation as investors bet on its solution for the industry's supply chain woes: factory-built data centers. Pixabay/The Digital Artist The Texas-based company intends to mass-produce 5-megawatt modular data center units that are built in factories and delivered by truck. Although the first units are still months away from production, Mavria has already raised $130M at a $1B valuation, The Wall Street Journal reported . Its investors include Paradigm, Liquid 2 and Critical Frontier, as well as public benefit corporation AMP. Mavria was founded this summer by Adam Blake, Nick Poradek and Seth Cohen, who met while working at the U.S. Department of Energy, where they focused on nuclear power. While at the department, the three say they identified a “strategic vulnerability” in the U.S.’s digital infrastructure build-out: strained supply chains, manufacturing capacity constraints and limited access to large blocks of power. Mavria’s business model is centered on the idea of addressing that problem through standardized, factory-built data centers. Its founders say this strategy can ease some of the physical supply chain bottlenecks that have contributed to data center construction continuing to trail significantly behind demand for these facilities. “Our power infrastructure, manufacturing capacity and supply chains are nowhere near ready to meet the demand from AI,” Blake told The Wall Street Journal. Mavria's modular product, which is branded as Terrain, consists of 5 MW units with power distribution, liquid cooling, control systems and server racks already integrated. The company describes Terrain as an effective plug-and-play data center system that can either be clustered with other modules to create a larger facility or be deployed individually to take advantage of locations where smaller pockets of grid capacity are available. The 35-employee startup is not yet producing units at scale. Its first units are being built at the company’s Houston factory, with plans to begin testing in 2027 before ramping up production later in the year. Mavria intends to pursue two business lines: selling the units directly and developing sites where Terrain systems could be deployed and operated. Beyond helping bypass supply chain constraints, its business model is appealing to investors because it can avoid the community opposition and political headwinds that are constraining large-scale data center development across the U.S. Paradigm Managing Director Alana Palmedo told The Wall Street Journal that while communities are pushing back against "mega projects," these modular units are less intrusive and can be deployed wherever small pockets of power are available. Mavria isn't the first firm to pursue modular solutions to the data center supply chain pinch. Modular, prefabricated components and off-site manufacturing have become essential strategies when building large-scale data centers, and an entire ecosystem of firms has emerged that manufacture shipping-container-sized, standalone data centers that can be deployed individually or grouped in larger installations. It’s a space that includes smaller edge specialists like Duos Edge AI and CenCore and major data center equipment manufacturers like Vertiv, Schneider Electric and Eaton Corp. items.title: NAR recommends new MLS policy changes amid Compass private-listings kerfuffle
items.description: NAR recommends new MLS policy changes amid Compass private-listings kerfuffle by John Yellig November 10, 2026 The National Association of REALTORS® recently issued four MLS policy recommendations aimed at modernizing MLS policies and improving client service. The recommendations come amid tension in the industry as some brokerages, Compass in particular, seek to disrupt the traditional MLS model with private listings , a move critics call monopolistic and anti-competitive. They also follow the creation of a shared listing platform by four of the nation's largest brokerages that seeks to combat Compass' Private Listing Network. NAR's four new policies seek to strengthen copyright protections for MLS listing content, provide MLSs with increased flexibility for establishing local data-feed requirements, clarify permitted uses of MLS data and update qualifications for service on NAR's MLS Committee. “These updates reflect our commitment to ensuring MLS policies remain relevant, effective and responsive to the needs of today's real estate industry,” NAR CEO Nykia Wright said. “In line with our 2026–2028 Strategic Plan and significant member feedback, we will continue working collaboratively with MLSs, brokers, members and other industry partners to support a clear understanding and implementation of these changes.” The recommendations include: The introduction of a new optional MLS policy, Copyright Protection of MLS Data, which provides MLSs the discretion to require up to a 50% copyright interest in certain listing content. Under the proposal, MLSs must provide participants with the right to opt-out of assigning a copyright interest to the MLS. Brokers retain the right to independently use and license their own listings. The establishment of an optional MLS policy about MLS Data Feed Services, which would provide MLSs with greater flexibility to establish local eligibility and licensing requirements for data feeds, provided they are applied equally to all participants, who retain access to their own MLS listings and data feeds. Establishing a new MLS Policy Statement to reinforce the fact that the use of MLS data must comply with applicable MLS participation or data licensing agreements and be connected to providing real estate brokerage services or preparing appraisals or other property valuations. This recommendation aims to help address concerns about unauthorized use of MLS content. Updating the qualification criteria for service on NAR's MLS Committee to better reflect today's MLS environment and ensure the committee continues to benefit from relevant industry expertise and perspectives. "This move seems proactive against the private listing threat by Compass," Miller Samuel Co-founder and housing analyst Jonathan Miller said. "The new policy lets MLSs base their feed eligibility on contributing listing content to the MLS. Firms can't take the benefits of access to all of the cooperative MLS listing content but then hide their own listings. "By bringing this up in advance, it will probably be easier for MLSs to cut off a Compass feed for not following their rules against hiding information," he concluded. items.title: Price per square foot is falling faster than the median in Phoenix. Bring that number to your next listing appointment.
items.description: Price per square foot is falling faster than the median in Phoenix. Bring that number to your next listing appointment. by Phoenix Agent November 09, 2026 Most Phoenix sellers walk into a listing appointment with one number already in their head. It usually came from a headline, a neighbor or a search portal, and it is almost always the median price. Right now, that number is telling them the market has barely moved. It isn't the whole story. Underneath a modest dip in the median, the value buyers place on each square foot of living space is slipping faster, and agents who build the pricing conversation around that figure will have an easier time explaining why a list price needs to land where it does. The gap is easy to see in the current numbers. According to Movoto's Phoenix market trends data, the median list price in the city is $455,000, down 2.2% from a year ago or roughly $10,000. Over the same stretch, the median price per square foot fell 3.8% to $278. Median home size, meanwhile, edged up 1% to 1,676 square feet. Put those three figures side by side and a pattern shows up. Part of what is holding the headline median steady is the mix of homes on the market, with somewhat larger homes making up more of what's listed. A bigger house at a lower price per foot can still post a respectable list price, and that makes the median look healthier than conditions really are for any single property. Sellers, understandably, don't think about their home as part of a mix. They think about it as their house, and they hear "down about 2%" as the discount they need to apply. Here is why that matters at the kitchen table. Take a 1,700-square-foot home and run simple math on the medians. At last year's implied rate of roughly $289 per square foot, it would have penciled out near $491,300. At today's $278, the same house comes in around $472,600, a difference of about $18,700. A seller who knocks 2.2% off last year's number to account for the market is only taking off about $10,800. That leftover $8,000 or so is often the difference between a listing that draws showings in its first two weeks and one that sits until the first price reduction. It's a simplified illustration rather than a valuation, but it makes the point in a way a seller can follow. Appraisers will be working at the per-foot level anyway. Fannie Mae's Selling Guide requires that adjustments to comparable sales reflect how the market actually responds to differences between properties, not a rule of thumb, and its own example involves adjusting for living area. If the list price was built on a stale headline figure and the appraisal is built on current per-foot evidence, the gap usually surfaces after a contract is signed, which is the worst possible moment to have that conversation. Supply is adding to the pressure. Movoto counts 6,068 active listings in Phoenix, up 17.3% year over year, with 448 new listings added in the past week alone. Demand, meanwhile, has been hesitant. Phoenix REALTORS®' September figures, as reported by ABC15 , showed pending sales in the city of Phoenix down 37% from a year earlier, even as new listings rose 2%. Pending sales are the closest thing agents have to a forward look, and a drop that size says buyers are taking their time and comparing carefully. Buyers who comparison-shop tend to notice price per square foot, even if they never say it out loud. None of this means every segment is soft. Mark Stapp, a real estate professor at Arizona State University , has noted that competition for homes under $450,000 remains strong, driven by a regional housing shortage that estimates put at around 56,000 units. That threshold sits almost exactly at the city's median list price, so a well-priced entry-level home can still move quickly. The per-foot lens helps here too. It shows a seller in that tier how much room they have, and it shows a seller of a larger home why they can't simply borrow the entry-level market's momentum. In practice, the conversation works best when it's visual. Before the appointment, pull the active homes for sale in Phoenix that match the seller's size range and neighborhood and calculate the list price per square foot for each. Then line those up against closed sales from the MLS over the last 90 days. Most sellers can see within a minute where their home sits relative to the competition, and the price recommendation stops feeling like the agent's opinion and starts looking like the market's. Price per square foot has limits, and it's worth saying so up front. Lot size, a pool, a casita, condition and age all move value in ways a single ratio can't capture, and smaller homes nearly always carry a higher per-foot price than larger ones. Comparing a 1,400-square-foot condo with a 2,600-square-foot single-family home on that basis will mislead everyone in the room. Keep comparisons within a similar size band and property type, and treat the number as a starting frame rather than a formula. The median will keep making headlines because it's simple and easy to report. Agents who bring the per-foot figure to the table get to have the honest pricing conversation on day one, before the market has it with their seller instead.
